_note: The root craft: 2 stones and 3 hours of grinding after discovering the cliff; personal completion unlocks descendants even when another sharp tool is already owned.

log: Holding one stone against another, you patiently grind away the rough surface until a usable cutting edge emerges.
After three hours of laborious work the stone has acquired an irregular but effective edge.
You first detach flakes with sharp blows, then refine the edge by grinding. It is a crude knife, but a serviceable one.
With the rough stone knife you labour over a straight branch until its end assumes a point.
The imperfect edge tears at the wood more than it cuts, but persistence eventually produces a spear.
Stroke after stroke, the stone blade removes enough wood to form a point fit for fishing.
You select a straight, sound branch and use the knife to shape its end into a sharp point.
A suitable branch is quickly reduced to a point with careful strokes of the knife.
Thin shavings fall from the wood as the knife gradually gives the branch the form of a spear.

_note: needs something sharp: the knife 30 min; the rock knife is slower (its tool.hoursFactor 2), with its own texts

log: You strike a hard stone until it bears a cutting edge, then secure it tightly in a split wooden haft.
After shaping a stone blade, you wedge it between the halves of a stout branch and bind them firmly.
A keen stone, a substantial handle, and patient binding together produce a simple axe.
You fasten a broad, flat stone crosswise to a wooden handle, fashioning a rudimentary hoe.
A flat stone and a sound handle are joined by cord until they form a tool for breaking soil.
The stone is bound firmly across the end of the haft. Crude though the hoe appears, it should turn the earth.

_note: Four bark strips twisted into rope; personal rock knife completion unlocks the recipe.

log: You twist strips of inner bark into three strands, then lay the strands together to obtain a stronger rope.
Hour after hour the fibres are braided until a length of serviceable rope lies coiled at your feet.
Under your fingers the bark becomes cord, and the cord becomes rope, though the labour leaves them sore.
